newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says considering talks with IMF on loan.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says considering talks with IMF on loan.

text.p: Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said on Thursday the government was considering talks with the IMF on securing a second year of a loan arrangement.
The IMF halted the first year of the three year $205 million ESAF loan last Thursday because of concerns over corruption.
In a statement issued in Nairobi, Mudavadi told the Kenyan public and investing community that the government was fully committed to pursuing sound fiscal and monetary policies.

"The government is considering initiating discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to negotiate for a reform programme under the second year ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility) arrangement, which, even after the lapsing of the first annual ESAF arrangement, is still available.
"This will provide the basis for continued sound macroeconomic management," Mudavadi said.

Mudavadi's statement followed the shilling falling four percent from Wednesday. It was quoted at a commercial average of 70.2 against the dollar at 2 p.m. (1100 GMT), compared with 67.50 at Wednesday's close.

The Central Bank of Kenya lists the previous all-time low at 69.22 but commercial banks say a central bank instrument that put a premium on the dollar in October 1993 meant real market rates reached 83.
Floor dealers on the Nairobi Stock Exchange said bonds, where foreign investors hold a huge stake, were under pressure, which was a major factor behind weakness of the shilling.
Mudavadi said the government was revising its budget to ensure expenditure was within available resources.
He added the government would also possibly accept higher interest rates for treasury bills to meet its requirements.

Mudavadi said results of the latest treasury bill tender opened by the central bank on Thursday showed that only 5.6 billion shillings of the 7.0 billion total advertised was bid for, leaving a shortfall of 1.4 billion shillings.
Current rates on benchmark 91-day treasury bills stand at 18.2 percent.
"I wish to assure the public, and, in particular the investing community, that the government is fully committed to pursuing sound fiscal and monetary policies," Mudavadi said.
"We are convinced that a stable macro-economic environment is key to our efforts to improve the quality of life of our people," Mudavadi added in his second statement this week.
He appealed to the business community not to "excessively adjust prices for their products" in order to support government efforts to maintain economic stability. ($1=70.2 Kenyan shillings)
